target: AG1's claim that animal dissection is educationally necessary because it is not required by standards or used in physician training
objection: The fact that AP Biology standards and Next Generation Science Standards do not require animal dissection, and that U.S. and Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training, suggests dissection is not necessary for the relevant educational goals.

target: AG1's claim that real animal dissection is needed for effective biology learning
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach anatomy, physiology, and related concepts equally well or better than dead animals, so animal dissection is unnecessary for student learning.

target: AG1's assumption that dissection is a harmless educational practice because animals are already dead
objection: Most dissection animals are reportedly caught in the wild, so dissection supply chains can harm local populations and biodiversity; the issue is not just whether the specimen is dead when used.

target: AG2's claim that lack of requirement by standards or medical schools shows dissection is inappropriate
objection: Biology standards specify learning goals rather than banning non-required teaching methods, and medical schools' physician-training practices are not a direct measure of what is appropriate in K-12 biology.

target: AG2's claim that animal dissection is unnecessary because alternatives are equally effective
objection: Animal dissection can support direct observation of real organs and tissues, which is itself a legitimate biology learning objective; standards not requiring dissection do not prove it is inappropriate.

target: AG1's claim that synthetic models cannot provide comparable hands-on skill practice
objection: Commercial synthetic anatomy materials can be physically cut and handled, and they are designed to mimic real tissue closely enough to provide comparable manual dissection practice and build fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination.

target: AG2's claim that synthetic models and simulations can replace dissection for all learning outcomes
objection: Synthetic models and simulations typically present idealized anatomy and do not expose students to the irregularities and individual variation found in real specimens, so they underrepresent authentic anatomical diversity.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives can replace dissection for laboratory competence
objection: Animal dissection teaches real-world lab and procedural skills, such as handling biological specimens and using dissection tools correctly, which synthetic models and simulations do not provide in the same way.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives make dissection unnecessary for motivating students
objection: Hands-on dissection can create 'aha moments' that spark interest in science careers, and inspiring students toward science is an important educational outcome, so dissection has motivational value beyond content learning.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives can replace dissection for critical thinking
objection: Real dissection forces students to observe actual anatomical evidence and infer structures and functions from it, whereas synthetic or virtual materials often provide more guided or pre-rendered information and thus less opportunity for the same evidence-based reasoning.

target: AG1's assumption that simulations lack the same evidence-generating discovery and inference demands as dissection
objection: Interactive virtual anatomy and simulation tools can require students to actively manipulate models, reveal structures, identify them, and infer relationships from their actions, so they can involve the same kinds of evidence-generation and inference.

target: AG2's claim that synthetic or simulation activities can replace dissection for learning 3D anatomical relationships
objection: Biology education requires understanding real three-dimensional structure-function relationships, and dissection uniquely lets students physically expose and trace real connections among tissues and organs rather than just view mediated representations.

target: AG1's assumption that only dissection can teach real three-dimensional anatomical relationships
objection: Some hands-on synthetic anatomy kits allow students to uncover internal structures and trace spatial connections, so non-animal alternatives can also support learning of 3D anatomical relationships.

target: AG1's claim that dissection supply chains do not cause biodiversity loss because specimens are already dead or byproducts
objection: Even if animals are dead when used, dissection supply chains can still involve wild-catching earlier in the process; if most dissection animals are caught in the wild, then the practice can still contribute to biodiversity loss.

target: AG2's claim that already-dead specimens do not matter if some animals were wild-caught earlier
objection: Over 98% of animals used for dissection were already deceased when provided, and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so school dissection typically does not depend on new wild-catching and therefore is not inherently tied to biodiversity loss.

target: AG1's claim that using already-dead or byproduct specimens avoids biodiversity harm
objection: If roughly 99% of dissection animals are wild-caught, then school demand can still incentivize wild-capture and biodiversity loss, even if some specimens are already dead when purchased.

target: AG1's claim that dissection is ethically and environmentally acceptable because specimens are already deceased/byproducts
objection: Even when specimens are already dead or byproducts, dissection purchases may still create demand that sustains wild-capture supply chains, so the practice can still have harmful environmental effects.

target: AG1's claim that dissection uniquely provides hands-on skill practice and science motivation
objection: Synthetic models, manufactured lab exercises, and engaging hands-on science activities can also develop fine-motor and hand-eye skills and create student motivation, so animal dissection is not uniquely necessary for those outcomes.

target: AG1's claim that already-dead/byproduct specimens make dissection ethically acceptable and educationally worthwhile
objection: Most dissection animals are reportedly wild-caught, so dissection supply chains can still cause biodiversity loss; claims that byproduct sourcing makes the practice harm-free are therefore undermined.

target: AG1's claim that animal dissection is a productive use of already-dead animals rather than a source of new harm
objection: Because dissection demand can increase wild-capture, it is not just reuse of waste; the practice can predictably contribute to biodiversity loss and is therefore not a harm-free productive use.

target: AG1's assumption that using already-dead animals avoids other harms
objection: Dissection often involves hazardous preservatives such as formaldehyde and hazardous chemical waste, so the practice creates additional health and environmental harms even when the animal was already dead.

target: AG1's claim that real dissection is necessary for anatomy and structure-function learning
objection: What students need for anatomy learning is to identify structures and infer relationships from anatomical evidence, and interactive virtual or synthetic alternatives can provide that evidence-based learning without cutting real animals.

target: AG1's claim that already-dead/byproduct sourcing makes dissection ethically acceptable
objection: Approximate 99% wild-capture rates mean dissection supply chains can still cause biodiversity loss, so the practice remains ethically and environmentally problematic even if some specimens are reused.

target: AG1's use of a decision rule that turns on whether dissection supply chains predictably contribute to biodiversity loss
objection: The premise that over 98% of specimens are already deceased does not defeat the claim that dissection supply chains may still involve wild-caught animals and thus still predictably contribute to biodiversity loss, so the anti-dissection condition can still be met.
